questLakeRuinsSixthQuests.questSeven: What do they recommend to use?

questLakeRuinsSeventhQuests.title: Forecast and Weather Changes
questLakeRuinsSeventhQuests.description: You discuss how the weather changes: clear, variable, temperature rises/falls during the day or night. You learn to understand temperature ranges.
questLakeRuinsSeventhQuests.goal: Understand and talk about the weather forecast
questLakeRuinsSeventhQuests.questNine: What’s the weather like during the day?

questLakeRuinsEighthQuests.title: Combine: Season, Weather, Degrees, Clothes
questLakeRuinsEighthQuests.description: You bring together all your weather knowledge: discuss which clothes fit windy and cold weather, and understand forecasts with temperatures by season.

questLakeRuinsNinthQuests.title: Planning the Day by Forecast
questLakeRuinsNinthQuests.description: You compare the morning/day/evening forecasts in different cities and decide if a jacket is needed. You learn to plan your day based on detailed weather forecasts.
questLakeRuinsNinthQuests.goal: Combine known words about weather and clothing

questLakeRuinsNinthQuests.questThirteen: Is a jacket needed during the day?

questLakeRuinsTenthQuests.title: Weekend Plans
questLakeRuinsTenthQuests.description: You look at the full weekend forecast, compare temperatures and decide where to go (park, museum), combining all your knowledge.

questsNorthCliffsFirstQuests.title: Booking and Check-in
questsNorthCliffsFirstQuests.description: You arrive at a hotel on the Northern Cliffs. You need to book and check in at the reception, asking for a single/double room and the price.

questsNorthCliffsSecondQuests.title: Questions at the Hotel Reception
questsNorthCliffsSecondQuests.description: You ask questions at the reception: about breakfast, Wi-Fi, and the elevator. You also ask for the bill and pay for the room.
questsNorthCliffsSecondQuests.questNine: How much is a double room?
questsNorthCliffsSecondQuests.questThirteen: How much is a late check-out?

questsNorthCliffsThirdQuests.title: Problems in the Room
questsNorthCliffsThirdQuests.description: There are issues in the room. You need to report a heating problem and ask for extra items or cleaning.
questsNorthCliffsThirdQuests.goal: asking for help with household issues

questsNorthCliffsFourthQuests.title: Services and Schedules
questsNorthCliffsFourthQuests.description: You are getting fully comfortable in the hotel. Now you need to find out the breakfast hours and make sure you know where the elevator and stairs are. You also ask if the parking is paid.

questsNorthCliffsFifthQuests.title: Check-out and Airport
questsNorthCliffsFifthQuests.description: It’s departure day. You need to pay the bill (cash/card), get the receipt, and return the key card. You ask to call a taxi to the airport and check if you can leave your luggage for storage.
questsNorthCliffsFifthQuests.goal: Taxi/airport, payment (cash/card), receipt/invoice, late check-out, leaving luggage, announcements

questsNorthCliffsFifthQuests.questFourteen: Build the phrase: This is my luggage

questsNorthCliffsSixthQuests.title: Trip and Hotel: Mini Dialogues
questsNorthCliffsSixthQuests.description: You practice using all learned hotel phrases: reservation, check-in, requests (towels), paying the bill, and going to the airport.
questsNorthCliffsSixthQuests.goal: Combine learned phrases: reservation, quiet room, breakfast times, elevator, bill/receipt, pay (cash/card), taxi/airport
questsNorthCliffsSixthQuests.questOne: For how many nights is the reservation?

questsNorthCliffsSeventhQuests.title: Hotel Dialogues
questsNorthCliffsSeventhQuests.description: Short, quick dialogues where you must respond instantly: room availability, Wi-Fi password, room problems, taxi request, and payment.

questsNorthCliffsEighthQuests.description: You go out into the city and decide to use public transport. You look for a stop or station, ask where the bus or subway goes, and buy a ticket.
questsNorthCliffsEighthQuests.goal: Use basic phrases in public transportation

questsNorthCliffsNinthQuests.title: Train: Station and Platforms
questsNorthCliffsNinthQuests.description: You are at the station. You learn to read the schedule: platform, departure, and arrival. You learn to ask about delays and transfers.
questsNorthCliffsNinthQuests.goal: Understand announcements and ask questions at the station
questsNorthCliffsNinthQuests.questFive: Build: The train departs from platform 4

questsNorthCliffsTenthQuests.title: Trip: Airport and Flight
questsNorthCliffsTenthQuests.description: You are at the airport. You go through check-in and security control, look for your boarding gate, and find where to collect your luggage.

questsNorthCliffsTenthQuests.questFifteen: Which gate should you go to?

questsNorthCliffsEleventhQuests.title: Trip: final practice
questsNorthCliffsEleventhQuests.description: You combine all your travel knowledge: hotel, transport, train station, airport. You reinforce the skills needed for independent travel.

questsNorthCliffsTwelfthQuests.description: The last set of mini-situations to feel confident using travel, booking, transport, and airport phrases.

questsStoneReachSecondQuests.title: In the Herbalist’s House
questsStoneReachSecondQuests.description: You are visiting an old herbalist. To stay, you must correctly name the rooms (kitchen, bedroom, bathroom) and basic furniture (bed, chair).
questsStoneReachSecondQuests.goal: Learn to name rooms and objects in the house.
questsStoneReachSecondQuests.questSix: Choose the correct phrase: This is a table
questsStoneReachSecondQuests.questSeven: Choose the correct phrase: This is a lamp

questsStoneReachThirdQuests.title: Colors Around
questsStoneReachThirdQuests.description: You start describing the objects around you using colors (red, blue, green, yellow).
questsStoneReachThirdQuests.goal: Learn to recognize phrases with colors and objects.

questsStoneReachThirdQuests.questThirteen: What does 'Der Teppich ist grün' mean?

questsStoneReachFourthQuests.goal: Understand phrases with numbers and objects: es gibt / ich habe / wie viele.

questsStoneReachFifthQuests.description: In the kitchen you learn the names of dishes (fork, spoon, plate, glass) and simple combinations with articles and adjectives.
questsStoneReachFifthQuests.goal: Learn kitchen items and simple phrases like Das ist / ein, eine, der, die, das.
questsStoneReachFifthQuests.questThird: How to say: This is a fork
questsStoneReachFifthQuests.questSeven: How to say: This is a spoon

questsStoneReachSixthQuests.description: You describe the living room: sofa, armchair, carpet, TV. You make simple descriptive sentences.

questsStoneReachSixthQuests.questFifteen: How to say: This is a carpet

questsStoneReachSeventhQuests.description: You learn bathroom vocabulary: shower, bathtub, sink, towel. You learn to talk about quantity (two towels) and quality (clean towel).
questsStoneReachSeventhQuests.goal: Name bathroom items and simple phrases with numbers and adjectives.
questsStoneReachSeventhQuests.questFive: Build the sentence: This is a shower

questsStoneReachEighthQuests.title: In the Bedroom
questsStoneReachEighthQuests.description: You describe the bedroom: bed, pillow, blanket, wardrobe, nightstand. You make phrases with adjectives (soft pillow).
questsStoneReachEighthQuests.goal: Name bedroom items and make simple sentences Das ist / ein, eine, der, die, das.
questsStoneReachEighthQuests.questFour: Build the sentence: This is a bed
questsStoneReachEighthQuests.questThirteen: Build the sentence: This is a mirror

questsStoneReachNinthQuests.title: In the Hallway
questsStoneReachNinthQuests.description: At the entrance, you learn words related to going out: door, key, jacket, coat, hat, shoes. You practice short descriptions of these items.
questsStoneReachNinthQuests.goal: Name hallway items and make short phrases with articles and numbers.
questsStoneReachNinthQuests.questFour: Build the sentence: This is a jacket
questsStoneReachNinthQuests.questSeven: Build the sentence: Two new shoes
questsStoneReachNinthQuests.questThirteen: Build the sentence: This is a door

questsStoneReachTenthQuests.goal: Name garden objects and make simple combinations with colors and numbers.

questsStormCoastsFourQuests.goal: Weihnachten, Ostern, Silvester, Neujahr, der Feiertag, Tradition, frei haben; simple date facts

preposition.title: All About German Prepositions
preposition.guideTitle: Your complete guide to one of the most important grammar topics

prepositionsIntro.title: What is a Preposition
prepositionsIntro.paragraph: A preposition is a function word that shows the relationship between words in a sentence and helps form correct structure. It usually comes before a noun or pronoun it refers to. In German, a preposition almost always requires the noun to be in a specific case (Dative, Accusative, Genitive).

prepositionsFirstBlock.title: Basic Meanings of Prepositions
prepositionsFirstBlock.description: They answer the questions "where?" and "to where?".
prepositionsFirstBlock.translateSecondPart: (on, at, to – vertical surfaces): Das Bild hängt
prepositionsFirstBlock.translateThree: (The book is lying on the table.)
prepositionsFirstBlock.translateFirstPartTwo: (on – for days of the week/times of day):
prepositionsFirstBlock.translateSecondPartTwo: (at – for specific times): Der Film beginnt
prepositionsFirstBlock.translateThirdPartThree: (We’re going to the sea in summer.)

prepositionsSecondBlock.title: Merging Prepositions with Articles
prepositionsSecondBlock.paragraph: Germans love to shorten! Prepositions often merge with the following article. You need to know and actively use these forms.

prepositionsThirdBlock.title: Most Important: Prepositions by Case
prepositionsThirdBlock.paragraph: This is the most important classification. You simply need to memorize the case required by each preposition.
prepositionsThirdBlock.twoWayTranslateFirst: The car is parked in front of the house.
prepositionsThirdBlock.twoWayTranslateSecond: I’m parking the car in front of the house.

adjectiveComparisonContentSide.ruleOne: To form the comparative (Komparativ), add -er. For the superlative (Superlativ), use the structure am + adjective + -sten.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.ruleTwo: Many short adjectives with (a, o, u) in the stem take an umlaut (ä, ö, ü) in comparative and superlative forms.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.ruleThree: Some important adjectives and adverbs have unique comparison forms or change their stem. You need to memorize them.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.firstThemeTipOne: 1. This is the basic rule and works for most adjectives.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.firstThemeTipTwo: 2. Use the comparative to compare two items: Er ist schneller als ich (He is faster than me).
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.firstThemeTipThree: 3. The superlative with “am” is used after a verb: Er läuft am schnellsten (He runs fastest of all).
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.firstThemeTipFour: 4. If the adjective stands before a noun, another form is used: der schnellste Mann (the fastest man).
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.practiceFirstDescription: Form comparative and superlative degrees for ordinary adjectives.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.secondThemeTipOne: 1. This rule mainly covers monosyllabic adjectives.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.secondThemeTipTwo: 2. Learn common ones: alt, groß, jung, kalt, warm, lang, kurz.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.secondThemeTipFour: 4. The adjective gesund follows this rule: gesund → gesünder → am gesündesten.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.practiceSecondDescription: Choose the correct form for adjectives that take an umlaut.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.thirdThemeTipOne: 1. These are exceptions—you can’t derive them, you must learn them.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.thirdThemeTipTwo: 2. gut, viel and gern are the most important and frequent exceptions.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.thirdThemeTipThree: 3. Note how hoch and teuer lose a vowel in the stem for easier pronunciation.
adjectiveComparisonContentSide.practiceThirdDescription: Test how well you know exception adjectives.

adjectiveContentSide.ruleFirst: If an adjective follows a definite article (der, die, das), which already shows the gender and case, the adjective takes the ending -e or -en.
adjectiveContentSide.ruleSecond: If an adjective follows an indefinite article (ein, eine) or a possessive pronoun (mein, dein), which doesn't always clearly indicate the gender or case, the adjective 'helps' and takes the 'strong' ending.
adjectiveContentSide.ruleThird: If there is no article before the adjective, it must show gender and case on its own. So it takes endings similar to definite articles.
adjectiveContentSide.firstThemeTipOne: 1. This is 'weak' declension. The article already shows everything, and the adjective 'is lazy'.
adjectiveContentSide.firstThemeTipTwo: 2. In most cases, use -en. It’s the most common and safest ending.
adjectiveContentSide.firstThemeTipThree: 3. Exception: use -e only in 5 singular cases — Nominative (der gute, die gute, das gute) and Accusative for feminine and neuter (die gute, das gute).
adjectiveContentSide.firstThemeTipFour: 4. Tip: if the article form is like in the Nominative (der, die, das), the ending is -e. If the article changes (den, dem, des), use -en.
adjectiveContentSide.FirstThemeTipTranslateThree: We are helping the young woman.
adjectiveContentSide.practiceFirstDescription: Test your knowledge of adjective endings after der, die, das.
adjectiveContentSide.secondThemeTipOne: 1. This is 'mixed' declension. First, check if the gender is clear from the article.
adjectiveContentSide.secondThemeTipTwo: 2. If the gender is UNCLEAR (Nominative masc. and neuter → ein Mann, ein Kind), the adjective takes the 'strong' ending: -er for masculine, -es for neuter.
adjectiveContentSide.secondThemeTipThree: 3. This also applies to Accusative neuter (ein Kind).
adjectiveContentSide.secondThemeTipFour: In ALL OTHER cases, the endings are the same as in 'weak' declension (mostly -en).
adjectiveContentSide.secondThemeTipTranslateFour: He is talking to a nice person.
adjectiveContentSide.practiceSecondDescription: Test your knowledge of adjective endings after ein, eine, mein, kein.
adjectiveContentSide.thirdThemeTipOne: 1. This is 'strong' declension. The adjective carries all the meaning.
adjectiveContentSide.thirdThemeTipTwo: 2. Tip: the adjective ending usually matches the last letter of the definite articles (der, die, das...).
adjectiveContentSide.thirdThemeTipThree: 3. This also applies to Accusative neuter (ein Kind).
adjectiveContentSide.thirdThemeTipFour: 4. Example: Dative feminine → article der → ending -er (mit gutER Laune).
adjectiveContentSide.thirdThemeTipFifth: 5. Important exception: in Genitive masculine and neuter, the ending is -en (not -es) to avoid double 's'.
adjectiveContentSide.practiceThirdDescription: Test your knowledge of endings when there is no article before the adjective.

perfectTips.first: 1. Important: 'haben' is used with actions, 'sein' with movement or state change
perfectTips.second: 2. Weak verbs: Partizip II = ge + stem + (e)t (e.g., gemacht, gelernt)
perfectTips.third: 3. Strong verbs: vowel change + -en ending (e.g., gesehen, gefahren)
perfectTips.fourth: 4. Separable prefix: ge goes inside (e.g., ankommen → angekommen)
perfectTips.fifth: 5. Inseparable prefix (ver-, be-, etc.): no ge (e.g., versprechen → versprochen)
perfectTips.sixth: 6. Auxiliary verb is conjugated; Partizip II goes to sentence end

prateritumTips.first: 1. Regular verbs: add endings -te, -test, -te, -ten, -tet, -ten to the stem
prateritumTips.third: 3. Irregular verbs: different stem (e.g., gehen → ging, sehen → sah)
prateritumTips.fourth: 4. Same endings used with the new stem
prateritumTips.fifth: 5. Unlike Perfekt, Partizip II and auxiliary verbs are not used

plusquamperfekt.first: 1. Plusquamperfekt = Präteritum of haben/sein + Partizip II
plusquamperfekt.second: 2. Example: hatte gemacht, war gegangen, hatte gesehen
plusquamperfekt.third: 3. Use of haben/sein is the same as in Perfekt
plusquamperfekt.fourth: 4. Partizip II is formed as usual: ge + stem + (e)t or irregular form

galaxyDescriptions.alpha: A sector ruled by three great powers: Der, Die, and Das. Your task is to calibrate your linguistic sensors and bring order to the grammatical system by flawlessly determining the gender of every word.
galaxyDescriptions.beta: An anomaly zone where everything multiplies and transforms. Study the laws of noun transformation to understand what form an object takes when there is more than one.
galaxyDescriptions.gamma: The galaxy of twin words. Expand your vocabulary by finding new ways to express the same thought. The more synonyms in your arsenal, the brighter your speech shines in deep space.
galaxyDescriptions.delta: A world of eternal contrast and opposition. Here, everything is known through comparison: from 'fast' to 'slow'. Learn to masterfully find opposites to maintain balance in the system.
galaxyDescriptions.epsilon: A time loop of the past. Master the complex form of verbs to write reports on completed missions and tell of your past victories in other star systems.
galaxyDescriptions.zeta: The navigation grid of space and time. Find out 'where', 'where to', and 'how' the linguistic paths lead. Correct prepositions are your precise coordinates in the infinity of language.

newsTitleBanner.title: Articles about the features of the German language, topic breakdowns, and useful knowledge to boost your level.

newsArticleOne.first: Do you eat chocolate when stressed or sad? Meet der Kummerspeck.
newsArticleOne.second: These are those exact extra pounds that persistently appear from worrying. Literally - 'bacon of grief'.
newsArticleOne.third: It consists of der Kummer (grief) and der Speck (bacon). As expected, this 'bacon' takes its gender from the article of the last noun.
newsArticleOne.cta: Admit it, have you ever had Kummerspeck?

newsArticleTwo.first: Know that sacred bliss when the workday is finally over? That's der Feierabend.
newsArticleTwo.second: Literally - 'celebration evening'. A special time of rest when even thinking about work is forbidden.
newsArticleTwo.third: It is made up of die Feier (celebration) and der Abend (evening). This pleasant time takes its gender from the article of the last noun — der Abend.
newsArticleTwo.cta: Do you always look forward to Feierabend at work?

newsArticleThree.first: German is the only major language in the world where absolutely all nouns are capitalized, regardless of their position in the sentence.
newsArticleThree.second: It doesn't matter if you're talking about a person, a dog, a regular chair, or an abstract thought — the first letter will always be uppercase. This often confuses beginners when learning.
newsArticleThree.third: However, this rule has a huge plus: when reading a German text, you can always accurately and at first glance identify exactly where an object is hidden in the sentence.

newsArticleFour.first: One of the most mind-blowing things about learning German is counting. Germans pronounce two-digit numbers from the end.
newsArticleFour.second: For example, they say the number twenty-one as 'one and twenty'. Because of this, when listening to spoken German, you have to mentally flip the digits in your head.
newsArticleFour.third: This linguistic trick often breaks the pattern for beginners, especially when they need to quickly write down a phone number or a price in a store by ear.
newsArticleFour.cta: Did you get used to this counting quickly, or do you still get confused?

newsArticleFive.first: In German, there is a strict word order rule that forces you to listen to your conversation partner until the very last word.
newsArticleFive.second: In certain types of sentences, the most important verb that indicates the action flies off to the very, very end.
newsArticleFive.third: You can build a long phrase and list a bunch of details, but your listener won't know if you bought, sold, broke, or lost the item until you utter the final word.
newsArticleFive.cta: Is it hard to rewire your thinking for this kind of word order?

newsArticleSix.first: When learning German, you will definitely panic sooner or later at the length of some words. The secret is that in German, there is officially no limit to the length of a noun.
newsArticleSix.second: You can endlessly glue words together, creating huge locomotives of letters just to describe a single object.
newsArticleSix.third: But the ultimate saving rule applies here: no matter how crazy the length of this monster is, it always takes its final grammatical gender from the article of the very last word.
newsArticleSix.cta: Do these long locomotive-words scare you?

newsArticleSeven.first: Does it ever happen that before an important event or sleep, you start playing out fictional scenarios and entire movies in your head in full detail? Germans describe this state as having your own cinema in your head.
newsArticleSeven.second: This is when your imagination or anxiety runs so wild that you literally get sucked into directing and watching your own thoughts.
newsArticleSeven.third: It is merged from der Kopf (head) and das Kino (cinema). This mental cinema obediently takes its final neuter gender from the article of the last noun.
newsArticleSeven.cta: Does this Kopfkino often turn on before you go to sleep?

newsArticleEight.first: The German language is full of self-irony when it comes to body shape. If you've gained a little extra weight on your sides, Germans won't talk about fat rolls; they will call it gold on the hips.
newsArticleEight.second: Literally, it translates to 'hip gold'. Such a delicate and precious description for love handles that got a bit rounder after delicious German sausages, buns, or beer.
newsArticleEight.third: The word consists of die Hüfte (hip) and das Gold (gold). Quite expectedly, this funny word takes its shiny neuter gender from the article of the last noun.
newsArticleEight.cta: How do you like such a poetic name?

newsArticleNine.first: Everyone knows what homesickness is, but Germans have a unique word for the exact opposite feeling. It is a longing for distant countries and travel.
newsArticleNine.second: Literally, it translates as 'distance-pain'. This is that exact aching feeling when you are sitting at home and unbearably want to go somewhere you have never been.
newsArticleNine.third: The word is assembled from die Ferne (distance) and das Weh (pain/woe). This romantic longing takes its final neuter gender from the article of the last word.
newsArticleNine.cta: Do you ever experience this kind of Fernweh?

newsArticleTen.first: Look at a regular electric light bulb. What shape does it remind you of? Germans saw a glowing fruit in it.
newsArticleTen.second: The literal translation of this word is 'glowing pear'. A very cozy, simple, and warm domestic description for a device we are so used to.
newsArticleTen.third: It comes from the verb glühen (to glow) and the noun die Birne (pear). Our light bulb takes its feminine gender from the article of the last word — die Birne.
newsArticleTen.cta: Does a light bulb look like a pear to you?

newsArticleEleven.first: How do you name that exact heavy emotional suffering when your love turns out to be unrequited? Germans combined these feelings into one expressive concept.
newsArticleEleven.second: Literally, it translates as 'love-grief'. This is a very accurate description for that longing and sadness that literally break your heart.
newsArticleEleven.third: The word is glued together from die Liebe (love) and der Kummer (grief). This broken heart obediently takes its masculine gender from the article of the very last word — der Kummer.
newsArticleEleven.cta: Is this feeling familiar to you?

newsArticleTwelve.first: Are you walking through the forest after the rain and notice a regular slug without a shell? The German language describes it in a highly stripped-down way.
newsArticleTwelve.second: The literal translation of this funny word is 'naked snail'. Indeed, why invent a new name if it's just a snail left without a house.
newsArticleTwelve.third: It is formed from the adjective nackt (naked) and the noun die Schnecke (snail). This forest dweller takes its feminine gender from the article of the last word.
newsArticleTwelve.cta: Did this name make you smile?

newsArticleThirteen.first: If you have ever learned English, we have great news for you. You already automatically know part of the German vocabulary, even if you have never specially studied it.
newsArticleThirteen.second: The thing is, English and German are close linguistic relatives from the same Germanic family. Words like brother, sister, water, green, or apple are written and sound incredibly similar.
newsArticleThirteen.third: This is precisely why learning German words with an English background is much faster — your brain subconsciously recognizes familiar patterns.
newsArticleThirteen.cta: Have you noticed the similarity between English and German?

newsArticleFourteen.first: The German letter eszett, which is written like a capital B, is a unique hallmark of the German alphabet. But when learning the language, few people know that by no means all German-speaking regions use it.
newsArticleFourteen.second: In Switzerland and Liechtenstein, this letter was officially and completely abandoned in the last century. In Swiss schools, newspapers, and official documents, they write the usual double 'ss' everywhere instead.
newsArticleFourteen.third: This happened due to the mass adoption of typewriters, where the Swiss simply didn't have enough space on the layout for both German and French characters simultaneously. Therefore, if you read Swiss texts, you won't find this letter there.
newsArticleFourteen.cta: Did you know about the Swiss secret of the German alphabet?

newsArticleFifteen.first: In German, there are amazing shape-shifter verbs that are spelled absolutely identically, but their meaning changes drastically depending on the stress. This fact often shocks beginners.
newsArticleFifteen.second: A prime example is the verb umfahren. If you stress the first part of the word, it means to knock over, hit, or run over an obstacle. But if you shift the stress to the second part, the word instantly changes to the opposite meaning — to drive around or bypass an obstacle.
newsArticleFifteen.third: This is precisely why, when learning such verbs, it is critically important to listen to where the stress falls; otherwise, during a practical driving lesson in Germany, you might accidentally terrify your instructor.
newsArticleFifteen.cta: Did you know about these tricky double-meaning verbs?

newsArticleSixteen.first: When foreigners don't understand what is being discussed, they usually say 'it's Greek to me.' Germans, however, apply pure railway logic in such a situation.
newsArticleSixteen.second: If a German completely fails to understand the speaker or doesn't want to listen to them, they will say: 'Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof' (I only understand train station).
newsArticleSixteen.third: Over time, the phrase turned into a popular idiom. Now, if someone is explaining directions too confusingly or overwhelming you with a complex topic, you can safely use this expression.
newsArticleSixteen.cta: Have you already heard this funny expression about the train station?

newsArticleSeventeen.first: Learning the articles der, die, das is an eternal headache for everyone learning German. But don't worry — sometimes even native speakers aren't sure about the correct choice of article.
newsArticleSeventeen.second: The realest and never-ending linguistic war in Germany unfolds every morning at breakfast around the famous Nutella chocolate spread. Germans have been arguing for decades about its grammatical gender.
newsArticleSeventeen.third: Some say die because it's a spread (creme), others think it's das since it's the neuter gender for foreign product names. The dispute escalated to such an extent that even the official Duden dictionary gave up and admitted that Nutella has no fixed article at all and any option can be used.
newsArticleSeventeen.cta: And which article would you give to Nutella?

newsArticleEighteen.first: If a person persistently fails to notice obvious things happening right under their nose, Germans won't say they are inattentive. They will find vegetables on their face.
newsArticleEighteen.second: The literal translation of this iconic idiom is 'to have tomatoes on one's eyes.' This is said about a driver who doesn't see a red light, or a friend who completely misses your hints.
newsArticleEighteen.third: The origins of the phrase date back to ancient courts, where the guilty were forced to wear blindfolds as a sign of shame, and sometimes real vegetables were tied to their eyes. Today, it's just a fun way to tell someone it's time to open their eyes.
newsArticleEighteen.cta: Have you already heard this phrase about tomatoes?

newsArticleNineteen.first: German textbooks teach us to greet people depending on the time of day: good morning, good afternoon, or good evening. But in northern Germany, they simply laugh at this system.
newsArticleNineteen.second: There, absolutely everyone uses one iconic word: Moin. The most interesting part is that you can say it absolutely anytime: at 8 AM to your boss, at 3 PM to a shop assistant, or late at night to friends at a bar. It simply means hello.
newsArticleNineteen.third: But be careful: if you decide to double the greeting and say 'Moin Moin,' the locals will immediately consider you a terrible chatterbox. In the north, they value brevity, so one word is more than enough.
newsArticleNineteen.cta: Have you already heard this greeting from people in Germany?

requestsLandSeven.questTask2: Build the sentence: “I’d like a tea, please”
requestsLandSeven.questTask3: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “I would like to pay”: Ich ___ bezahlen.
requestsLandSeven.questTask4: Choose the correct option: “We’d like two pieces of cake”
requestsLandSeven.questTask5: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “What would you like?”: Was ___ du?
requestsLandSeven.questTask6: What would the guest like to drink?
requestsLandSeven.questTask7: Build the sentence: “I would like a roll with cheese”
requestsLandSeven.questTask8: Choose the translation: “What would you like? (polite form)”
requestsLandSeven.questTask9: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “He would like a slice of pizza”: Er ___ ein Stück Pizza.
requestsLandSeven.questTask10: Choose the correct option: “I’d like a kilo of apples”
requestsLandSeven.questTask11: Fill in the missing word. “I would like the bill”: Ich möchte die ___.
requestsLandSeven.questTask12: How much cheese does the customer want?
requestsLandSeven.questTask13: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “Could you help me?”: ___ Sie mir helfen?
requestsLandSeven.questTask14: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “Take the money!”: ___ das Geld!
requestsLandSeven.questTask15: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “We wanted to go to the cinema”: Wir ___ ins Kino gehen.

requestsLandEight.questDescription: We check all kinds of requests and review the past tense and prepositions from earlier lands.
requestsLandEight.questTask1: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “Come tomorrow!”: ___ morgen!
requestsLandEight.questTask2: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “Children, eat!”: Kinder, ___!
requestsLandEight.questTask3: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “Please wait! (polite form)”: ___ Sie bitte!
requestsLandEight.questTask4: Fill in the missing word. “Open the door!”: Mach die Tür ___!
requestsLandEight.questTask5: Choose the correct option: “Can you help me? (polite form)”
requestsLandEight.questTask6: Build the sentence: “Could you close the door?”
requestsLandEight.questTask7: Choose the translation: “I’d like a pizza”
requestsLandEight.questTask9: Fill in the verb in the correct form. “Where were you?”: Wo ___ du?
requestsLandEight.questTask10: Choose the correct option: “I could not come”
requestsLandEight.questTask11: Fill in the short form of preposition and article. “My birthday is in May”: Mein Geburtstag ist ___ Mai.
requestsLandEight.questTask12: Fill in the short form of preposition and article. “I am coming from the doctor”: Ich komme ___ Arzt.
requestsLandEight.questTask13: Fill in the preposition. “The lamp is next to the bed”: Die Lampe steht ___ dem Bett.

wisdom-summit.p1: Review everything from the Lands of the Wise
wisdom-summit.p2: Each trial: one topic from the earlier lands
wisdom-summit.p3: At the end: the exam for all of B1
wisdom-summit.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

opinion-tower.p1: Opinion: Ich finde, dass…, Meiner Meinung nach ist…
opinion-tower.p2: Yes or no: Da hast du recht. Das stimmt nicht.
opinion-tower.p3: A guess: Er wird wohl krank sein. vielleicht, wahrscheinlich, bestimmt
opinion-tower.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

word-forge.p1: Nouns: wohnen → die Wohnung, gesund → die Gesundheit, möglich → die Möglichkeit
word-forge.p2: Adjectives: der Tag → täglich, die Sonne → sonnig, essen → essbar
word-forge.p3: The opposite with un-: möglich → unmöglich, gesund → ungesund
word-forge.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

nuance-bridge.p1: Shades of meaning: zwar… aber, sowohl… als auch, indem, bis
nuance-bridge.p2: Passiv Perfekt and participles: ist gebaut worden, die geöffnete Tür
nuance-bridge.p3: No need, somewhere, they say: brauchen nicht zu, irgendwo, Er soll reich sein
nuance-bridge.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

link-harbor.p1: Pairs: nicht nur… sondern auch, entweder… oder, weder… noch
link-harbor.p2: The more…, the…: Je mehr ich lerne, desto besser spreche ich
link-harbor.p3: statt… zu (instead of), seitdem, bis, sobald
link-harbor.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

question-bridge.p1: Verb + its own preposition: warten auf, denken an, sich interessieren für
question-bridge.p2: About a person: Auf wen? auf ihn. About a thing: Worauf? darauf
question-bridge.p3: A whole clause: Ich freue mich darauf, dass du kommst
question-bridge.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

taste-market.p1: No article: the adjective shows the ending itself (heißer Kaffee)
taste-market.p2: Like the article: der → guter, das → kaltes, dem → mit heißem, der → mit frischer
taste-market.p3: viele junge Leute, wegen schlechten Wetters, ads and menus
taste-market.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

hero-square.p1: Weak nouns: der Kollege, but den / dem / des Kollegen
hero-square.p2: Which ones: people and animals ending in -e, der Mensch, der Herr, words ending in -ent, -ant, -ist
hero-square.p3: Only the subject has no -n: Der Junge spielt. A special word: des Namens
hero-square.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

owner-castle.p1: Whose? des (masculine and neuter), der (feminine and plural)
owner-castle.p2: meines, meiner, eines; Annas Auto; in speech von + dative
owner-castle.p3: Prepositions with the genitive: wegen (because of), trotz (despite), während (during)
owner-castle.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

regret-river.p1: If back then: hätte gemacht, wäre gekommen
regret-river.p2: Full condition: Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, wäre ich gekommen
regret-river.p3: Now (würde kommen) and back then (wäre gekommen)
regret-river.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

wish-island.p1: Unreal: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich reisen (if I had)
wish-island.p3: Ich wünschte, … and the difference: habe (real) and hätte (unreal)
wish-island.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

experience-summit.p1: Review everything from the Mountains of Experience
experience-summit.p2: Each trial: one topic from the earlier lands
experience-summit.p3: At the end: the exam of the Mountains of Experience
experience-summit.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

decision-workshop.p1: Decisions and questions: eine Entscheidung treffen, eine Frage stellen
decision-workshop.p2: Letting someone know and being informed: Bescheid sagen, Bescheid wissen
decision-workshop.p3: Being considerate, suggesting, talking: Rücksicht nehmen, einen Vorschlag machen, ein Gespräch führen
decision-workshop.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

task-tower.p1: zu + infinitive at the end: keine Lust zu kochen
task-tower.p2: Es ist schwer, … zu …; versuchen, vergessen, ohne … zu (it is hard, try, forget, without)
task-tower.p3: lassen: someone else does it (Ich lasse mein Auto reparieren)
task-tower.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

craft-valley.p2: Who does it: von + dative (vom Mechaniker)
craft-valley.p3: Past and modals: wurde, muss … werden
craft-valley.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

neighbor-street.p1: Who / which: der, die, das (by the gender of the noun)
neighbor-street.p2: Case: den (whom?), dem and denen (to whom?)
neighbor-street.p3: With a preposition and was: in dem, mit dem, alles, was
neighbor-street.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

consequence-fork.p1: Result: sodass and so … dass (so, so … that)
consequence-fork.p2: Goal or result: damit or sodass
consequence-fork.p3: Condition and duration: falls (in case) and solange (as long as)
consequence-fork.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

purpose-path.p2: Different people: damit (so that you, so that he)
purpose-path.p3: Asking about a goal: wozu? (what for?)
purpose-path.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

reason-bridge.p2: Giving a reason three ways: weil, denn and deshalb
reason-bridge.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

memory-lake.p1: Plusquamperfekt: hatte gemacht, war gegangen (what had happened before)
memory-lake.p2: nachdem and bevor: what came before and after
memory-lake.p3: während: two actions at the same time, and a story with all tenses
memory-lake.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

story-valley.p1: Präteritum for telling stories: machte, ging, kam, fuhr, las
story-valley.p2: Mixed verbs and verbs with prefixes: brachte, dachte, stand auf, kam an
story-valley.p3: Als and wenn in the past, and telling a story in order: zuerst, dann, danach, am Ende
story-valley.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

a2-summit.p1: Review of the past tense, cases and prepositions
a2-summit.p2: Subordinate clauses, adjective endings and plans for the future
a2-summit.p3: Requests, advice, comparison and the final A2 exam
a2-summit.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

nobody-village.p1: Someone and no one: jemand, niemand. Something and nothing: etwas, nichts
nobody-village.p2: Everything: alles. People in general: man (Hier darf man nicht rauchen)
nobody-village.p3: Instead of a noun: einer, keiner, meiner, deiner
nobody-village.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

choice-crossing.p1: Which one? welcher, welche, welches. This: dieser, diese, dieses
choice-crossing.p2: Every: jeder, jede, jedes. All: alle
choice-crossing.p3: What kind of? Was für ein …? Short answer: Der hier. Den da.
choice-crossing.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

advice-garden.p1: Advice with sollte: Du solltest mehr schlafen
advice-garden.p2: Wishes: Ich würde gern …, Ich wäre gern …, Ich hätte gern …
advice-garden.p3: Suggestions and questions: Würdest du …? Wie wäre es mit …? An deiner Stelle würde ich …
advice-garden.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

comparison-hills.p1: Comparative: schneller, älter, größer and the word als
comparison-hills.p2: Special forms (gut, viel, gern) and so … wie
comparison-hills.p3: Superlative: am schnellsten and der schnellste Zug
comparison-hills.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

time-road.p1: Ago: vor + dative: vor zwei Jahren, vor einer Woche
time-road.p2: Since, still going: seit drei Jahren. For a period: für eine Woche
time-road.p3: In (future): in einer Stunde. After and before: nach dem Essen, vor dem Essen. From and until: ab Montag, bis Freitag
time-road.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

calendar-valley.p1: Ordinal numbers: erste, zweite, dritte … zwanzigste
calendar-valley.p2: Dates: Heute ist der dritte Mai. Am dritten Mai …
calendar-valley.p3: Time: halb vier, Viertel nach drei, um 15 Uhr
calendar-valley.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

a1-summit.p3: The A1 exam, and then A2
a1-summit.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

healer-hut.p1: What hurts: Mein Kopf tut weh. Meine Beine tun weh.
healer-hut.p2: Symptoms: Ich habe Fieber und Husten.
healer-hut.p3: At the doctor’s: Sie müssen im Bett bleiben.
healer-hut.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

dress-bazaar.p1: What I wear: Ich trage eine Hose. Sie trägt ein Kleid.
dress-bazaar.p2: I like it: Das Kleid gefällt mir. Gefällt dir die Jacke?
dress-bazaar.p3: In the shop: Die Hose passt gut. Ich nehme sie.
dress-bazaar.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

hearty-inn.p1: What I like: Ich mag Käse. Ich esse gern Pizza.
hearty-inn.p2: How much: eine Tasse Kaffee, ein Glas Wasser
hearty-inn.p3: At the restaurant: Ich nehme die Suppe. Die Rechnung, bitte!
hearty-inn.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

power-pass.p1: The second verb goes to the end: Ich kann gut schwimmen
power-pass.p2: Four verbs: können, müssen, wollen, dürfen
power-pass.p3: With a prefix: Ich muss früh aufstehen
power-pass.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

routine-mill.p1: The prefix goes to the end: aufstehen → Ich stehe früh auf
routine-mill.p2: My day: aufstehen, einkaufen, aufräumen, fernsehen
routine-mill.p3: Travel: Der Zug fährt ab. Er kommt um zehn Uhr an.
routine-mill.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

clock-tower.p1: Days of the week: am Montag, am Wochenende
clock-tower.p2: The time: Es ist acht Uhr. Um neun Uhr.
clock-tower.p3: Months and seasons: im Mai, im Sommer
clock-tower.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

family-tree.p1: My and your: mein Vater, meine Mutter, dein Kind, deine Eltern
family-tree.p2: His, her, our, your: sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr
family-tree.p3: In the Akkusativ like einen: Ich besuche meinen Opa
family-tree.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

change-river.p1: Vowel a → ä: fahren → du fährst, er fährt
change-river.p2: e → i and e → ie: essen → er isst, lesen → sie liest
change-river.p3: wir, ihr, sie stay regular: wir fahren, ihr esst
change-river.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

market-square.p1: Whom? What? The masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen
market-square.p2: die, das and the plural stay the same
market-square.p3: At the market and in the shop: ein Kilo Äpfel, Das macht zehn Euro
market-square.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

question-gorge.p1: Yes/no question: the verb comes first. Wohnst du hier?
question-gorge.p2: Question word: wer, was, wo, woher, wie + verb. Wo wohnst du?
question-gorge.p3: “No”: nicht for a verb or quality, kein for a thing. Ich bin nicht müde. Ich habe kein Auto.
question-gorge.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

meet-meadow.p1: Who? ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie
meet-meadow.p2: To be and to have: ich bin, du bist, ich habe, du hast
meet-meadow.p3: The verb changes its ending: ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt
meet-meadow.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

east-plain.p1: Say hello and goodbye: Hallo, Guten Tag, Tschüss
east-plain.p2: Talk about yourself: Ich heiße Anna. Ich komme aus Spanien.
east-plain.p3: Numbers, prices and the café: Ein Kaffee, bitte. Das kostet drei Euro.
east-plain.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

landIntro.intro: Hi! Here’s what we’ll learn here:
landIntro.introGrammar: Hi! Here we work on grammar:

stone-reach.p1: Name rooms, furniture and things at home together with their gender
stone-reach.p2: Describe things: colour, size, new or old
stone-reach.p3: Count things and talk about them in the plural

wind-valley.p1: Name places in the city: streets, transport, shops and cafés
wind-valley.p2: Explain where things are: next to, opposite, in front of, behind, between
wind-valley.p3: Ask for directions and explain the way: left, right, straight on

lake-ruins.p1: Talk about the weather: sun, rain, snow, wind and fog
lake-ruins.p2: Name the seasons and temperature and understand a forecast
lake-ruins.p3: Choose clothes for the weather and plan your day and weekend

north-cliffs.p1: Book a room, check in and check out of a hotel
north-cliffs.p2: Sort out problems at the hotel: internet, towels, heating
north-cliffs.p3: Find your way at the station and airport: tickets, platforms, flights
north-cliffs.p4: At the end: final practice with the hotel, transport, station and airport together

storm-coast.p1: Invite people to a party, accept or politely say no
storm-coast.p2: Congratulate people, give gifts and name the main holidays of the year
storm-coast.p3: Plan a party: date, time, food, drinks and dress code
storm-coast.p4: Family celebrations (weddings, anniversaries, christenings) and final practice

master-lands.p1: Talk about work: jobs, colleagues, the working day and breaks
master-lands.p2: Name tools, loads and safety rules at the warehouse and building site
master-lands.p3: Handle work matters: being late, holidays, salary, contracts and sick leave

wild-lands.p1: Name nature around you: forests, mountains, lakes, the sea and meadows
wild-lands.p2: Talk about animals and birds and what they do
wild-lands.p3: Describe the weather, morning, evening and the night sky

future-land.p2: How a future-tense sentence is built and where the verb goes
future-land.p3: Plans, predictions and promises in the future tense

past-land.p1: The Perfekt past tense, the main past tense in spoken German
past-land.p2: How to form the Partizip II of regular, strong and prefixed verbs
past-land.p3: Which helper verb to use: movement and change of state need a different one

action-valley.p1: The Dativ and Akkusativ cases: “me, you, him” and the order “first to whom, then what”
action-valley.p2: Prepositions with Dativ, with Akkusativ, and “where / where to” prepositions that switch case
action-valley.p3: Verbs that demand their own case or preposition, and pronominal adverbs that replace a whole phrase with one word
action-valley.p4: At the end: a final mix of cases, prepositions and replacements

order-valley.p1: Subordinate clauses: the verb goes to the very end
order-valley.p2: Linking words “because”, “that”, “if”, “although”, “so that” and question words, also with modal verbs and the Perfekt
order-valley.p3: The phrase es gibt (“there is / there are”) and the Akkusativ after it
order-valley.p4: Reflexive verbs: when the pronoun is Akkusativ and when Dativ. Then everything together on travel, work and home

time-gate.p1: Tense review: the Perfekt past and the Futur I future
time-gate.p3: Subordinate clauses on everyday topics: city, work, holidays, shopping, health

edge-images.p1: Adjective endings after the definite article
edge-images.p2: The adjective endings -e and -en: when to use which
edge-images.p3: All cases and the plural in sentences with the Perfekt and Futur I

secret-lands.p1: Adjective endings after the indefinite article
secret-lands.p2: The adjective endings -er, -es, -e and -en: when to use which
secret-lands.p3: Adjectives in the Nominativ, Akkusativ and Dativ in sentences with the Perfekt and Futur I

definite-indefinite.p1: Definite and indefinite articles: what’s the difference
definite-indefinite.p2: Adjective endings after both kinds of article, mixed together
definite-indefinite.p3: Spaced repetition so the rule sticks for a long time

place-prepositions.p1: Prepositions of place: in, on, under, above, in front of, behind, next to, between
place-prepositions.p2: The question “where?” and the Dativ after prepositions of place
place-prepositions.p3: Merging a preposition with the article, and “my, your” after prepositions of place
place-prepositions.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

direction-prepositions.p1: Prepositions of direction: going to a person, a city, a country, home
direction-prepositions.p2: Prepositions for “at someone’s place” and “from where”
direction-prepositions.p3: Compare “where to”, “where” and “where from”, learn “with whom / by what”. All these prepositions take the Dativ
direction-prepositions.p4: At the end: a final test that also reviews topics from earlier lands

action-prepositions.p1: Prepositions with Akkusativ (“for”, “without”, “through”, “around”) and with Dativ (“opposite”, “past”)
action-prepositions.p2: Prepositions of time: day, hour, month and season
action-prepositions.p3: Prepositions of periods: “from … to”, “starting from”, “for / since”, “… ago”, “after”
action-prepositions.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

past-simple.p2: Modal verbs in the Präteritum: could, had to, wanted to, was allowed to
past-simple.p3: Word order with modal verbs in the past tense
past-simple.p4: At the end: a review of the whole land and a final test with topics from earlier lands

requests-land.p1: The imperative (Imperativ): for one friend, for several people and the polite form
requests-land.p2: Requests with separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end
requests-land.p3: Polite requests as questions (“can you…?”, “could you…?”) and ordering politely with “I would like…”
requests-land.p4: At the end: a final test that also reviews topics from earlier lands

dictation.title: Dictation
dictation.infoText: Listen to the phrase and write it in German. Punctuation does not matter, but umlauts (ä, ö, ü), ß and capital letters on nouns do! The turtle button reads more slowly.
dictation.marks: ⚠️ Almost! Check the umlauts and capital letters
dictation.wrong: ❌ There are mistakes, compare with the correct answer
